I followed into a burying ground, in the subuios of the city, a small train of persons, not more than a dozen, w ho had come to bunone of their acquaintance. The clergyman in attendance, was lending a little hoy by the hand who seemed to be the only relative of the deceased in the slender group. 1 gathered with them round the grave, and 'when the plain coffin was lowered down, the child burst forth in uncontrolable grief. The little fellow had no one left to whom he could look for a flection, or who could address him in tones of parental kindness. The last of his kinsfolk was in the þÿgrave and he was alone. When the clamorous grief of the child had a little subsided, the clergyman addressed us with the customary exhortation to accept the monition, and be prepared; and turning to the child he added, þÿ She is not to remain in this grave forever ; as true as the grass which is now chilled with the frost of the season, shall spring to greenness and lilb in a few months, so true shall your mother come from that grave to another life, to a life up of happiness 1 þÿhope. The attendants shovelled m the earth upon the coffin, and some one took little William, the child, by the hand, and led him forth from the lowly tenement of his mother.

What a faithful watch keeper þÿ what mother would desire a richer monument than the form of her only son bending tearful, hut hoping, over her grave ? þÿ But,þÿWilliam, said I, þÿ is it in another world that she will þÿarise, þÿ and 1 attempted to explain to him the nature of that promise which he had mistaken. THE BARBADIAN. Bridge-town, September 4, 1839. It is a melancholy truth that the infection of Small Pox still exists in that quarter, where it first appeared when the man John Padmore went, in a fatal moment, from on board the Glengary, to Hopeland plantation. Seventeen days, it will be remembered, from the day he left Hopeland to be placed on board the Quarantine vessel, this man's cousin, Ned Padmore, was seized with illness at the adjoining Estate Waterford, and died, þÿ not of the Small Pox as his medical attendant declared, but of hemorrhage þÿ hut, before he expired, he w is so covered with pustules as to be in a most deplorable slate. Not the slightest doubt is entertained by the medical men that he had Small Pox. Since then a young woman, at Friendship, also an adjoining estate to life land, has died of the disease; and now, another case, that of a child, and that child, we arc informed, the daughter of John Pudmore, is ill with Small Pox. From the New York Commercial Advertiser. Financial Prospects. þÿ The following letter. from a London correspondent of the Courier and Enquirer, expresses very nearly our own opinion touching the existing financial crisis in England ; and we readily adopt instead of writing another article advancing the same ideas, as we were preparing to do when this letter came before us : Cori espondence oj the Courier. London. July 5, 1839. After the favorable accounts of the cotton market taken out by the Liverpool, you will scarcely be prepared for the disastrous news by the Great Western. Not only is the cotton interest i i a manner prostrated, but such is deemed the da r of a suspension of specie payments bv the Bank of England, that the governors of that institution boldly and openly avow the,- determination to raise the rate of interest to six and even seven per cent, if necessary to depress the pi ices of every description of manufactured goods, and thus invite cash purchasers from the continent. It will scarcdv be credited in the United States, and yet it is a matter of public notoriety here, that in this good city of London, where money is usually worth but three and three and a half per cent, per annum, hundreds of thousands of pounds sterling have been loaned for sixty days on Government Exchequer bills and Consols þÿ the very best security known in this market þÿ at the rate of one and a half per cent, per month, or eighteen per cent, per annum ! Indeed 1 have been in-

formed bv one of the most eminent bankers in the city, that cases are known where two per cent, a month has been paid for money, on a hypothecation of rail road shares at a valuation which rendered them as good security as consols. 1 need not say that this is a state of things which has never before been known in this country, and which cannot fail to suspend all operations in American stocks. Fortunately, the amount of hypothecated and not actually sold, is small ; and, consequently, the amount to be provided for will not materially afiect us. But the amount of cotton still in the hands of our countrymen, is estimated at nearly a million of bales ; and at the existing low prices will cause an absolute loss of one fourth the whole cost of this very large amount, Much pecuniary distress must necessarily follow among the holders of cotton and all connected with them ; but 1 am unwilling to believe that it will necessarily result in a general failure of those concerned in the article. Fortunately for our country, there has been much caution and prudence exercised by our commercial community since the resumption of specie payments ; and although there is great reason to suppose that specie must be sent to makeup the deficiency in the value of our cotton, yet we have more than we want for the current business of the country, and as its only value is in making up the deficiency occurring from time to time in our commercial transactions with this country, it is to be hoped that no panic will

arise from seeing it applied to its legitimate purpose. The suffering on this side of the Atlantic is destined to be severe beyond any thing heretofore known in this country : and this will not be the consequence of a suspension of specie payments by the 13uuk of England, but

T23"J2IT1>33X t&ZaiatftKTOS £.733. of the firm and energetic measures resorted to by that institution to prevent a suspension. The short crop of last season has reduced the bullion in her vaults to less than four millions and a half, some of which is silver, and of which it is admitted that only about three millions are available, ller restrictive measures have now been in operation nearly two months, during which the drain upon her has continued steady at the rate of about £800, 000 per month. But 1 am happy to add that from all appearances, the current is about turning in her favor, & in despite of the rabid articles in the Times, and its confident prediction that a suspension of cash payments will take place, no such eventneed be apprehended. Already gold has ceased to flow from her into France ; and it is now well ascertained, that the last shipment of gold to Hamburgh resulted in a clear loss. This being the case, the Bank will daily gadually but certainly increase its stock of bullion on hand ; and that too, without resorting to another advance on the rate of interest. It was confidently expected that the rate would have been advanced to six per cent, yesterday, the intelligence from Hamburgh, however, rendered such a measure unnecessaiy. But it must not be supposed that because gold has already, or will shortly commence flowing back into England, the Bank will im_ mediately relax in its present course. Far from it. It is said in the Bank parlor and promulgated through the city, that the price

of cottons, woollen, (St indeed every species of manufactured goods is too high þÿ and that until they are reduced, and the cupidity of the foreign purchaser thus excited to invest in these articles, and thus return the bullion taken away bv the introduction of foreign bread stuffs, no relaxation, no change in the Bank policy, need be anticipated. With the propriety or policy of this measure 1 have nothing to do Its eflec.t will be to bankrupt hundreds here, while it must inevitably keep down the price of our cotton, and render all our securities unsaleable.

Ou RACE þÿ Negro Sam, the property of Mr. Wilson, Trigg county Kentucky, has of been tried, found guilty, and received sentence of death during the present term id the Christian circuit court, for violence upon the person of a Mrs. Hill, of this county. But few instances can be found in the history of crime, of a wretch so daring and persevering in villanous efibrts, as this negro has been. About one o'clock at night, during the last days of April, Mrs. Hill, whose family consisted ol a little brother, nine or ten years old, and a small child or two of her own, was roused from her sleep by a noise in her room. She discovered that some person was in the room, and called upon the intruder to state his object. The negro replied in a manner that left her no ground to doubt ot her perilous situation. In the same moment she oidered the negro to withdraw, and directed her little brother to light a candle. The negro threatened the boy with death if he struck a light, and immediately proceeded to the bed of Mrs. Hill, and being a large and powerful man, he easily accomplished his diabolical purpose upon the agonized and resisting woman who is of a weak and delicate frame. The negro then left the house, when the unhappy woman barred the door, hoping to escape further injury. In a short time, however, the wretch returned and directed her to opcu the door. She begged him to depart.

He refused to do so, and 'proceeded to fore® the door, when she escaped from the house by some other outlet than that which the negro guarded. He however discovered her from the glare of vivid streams of lightning w hich were flashing through the sky, pursued her, caught her, and forced her to an out house, from which place the poor woman was not released until morning, and perhaps only saved her life bv telling the negro that she did not know him. Early in the morning she detailed the events of the night to a neighbor, whose house she sought. The villain was immediately chased, caught, and lodged in jail, from which he broke in a few days, and shifted his haunts to another neighborhood, fifteen or twenty miles from the scene of his crime. After being at liberty a few days he went to the house of a man by the name ofDeason, and informed him that his (Reason's) mother, who lives at some considerable distance from Reason's was very sick and desired to see him. The credulous man started to see his mother, when the lawless negro forthwith entered the house. M rs. Reason became alarmed and fled. The villain followed and caught her. Mrs. Reason being a large and strong woman, resisted this modern J'luto lonff, with a hope of saving herself from the untimely purpose of her assailant; but she was finally overpowered, when the fellow left her. He was, however, quickly secured, and now awaits his doom. He is to be hanged the 7th July. þÿ Hopkins ville Gazette.

American Hail Roads. þÿ The Chevalier de Gerstner who constructed a rail road of 130 miles in Austria, and another in Russia, has, during the past year, made a thorough examination of our rail roads in the United States. He says in a brief report he has recently published west. According to the facts collected during my travels since mv arrival in New York, there are now over three thousand miles of Rail Roads now completed and in operation in the United States ; 4'25 locomotives, of which the greatest number were made in this country, run on the several rail roads, and I believe that up to the end of 1839, the length of rail roads in the United Stales may amount to ii (hi miles. The capital expended on the Rail Roads now in operation, is about sixty millions of dollars, or at any average cost of twenty thousand dollars per mile, for which sum the Rail Roads with the buildings have been constructed and the necessary locomotives and cars bought. Of the courtesies he received from all the different companies, he says that : The presidents, directors, and engineers of the different rail road lines, had given him not only their printed reports, but had laid before him with the greatest liberality their books and accounts, in order to give him every kind of information. To which he adds : I fulfil only my duty, when 1 publicly acknowledge that such a liberality is only to be found amongst a free and enlightened people, where ail public works are based on the prin-

The latter jokingly observed that she had promised her sweetheart that no man should kiss Iter while absent It being holiday time, Saverland considered this a challenge, and caught hold of her and kissed her. The young woman took it as a juke but her sister, the defendant said she would like as little of that kind of fun as he pleased. Saverland told her, if she was angry he would kiss her also ; he then tried to do it, and they tell to the ground. On rising, the woman struck him, he again tried to kiss her, and in the scuffle she bit off' his nose, which she spit out of her mouth J'he action was brought to recover damages for the loss of the nuse. i he defendant said he had no business to kiss her. If she wanted kissing she had a husband to kiss ker, a better looking man than ever trie prosecutor was. Making a flood Title. A very curious mode of trying the title to land is practised in llindostan. Two holes are dug in the disputed spot in each of which the plaintiffs and the defendant's lawyers put one of their legs, till one ol them is tired, nr complains of being stung by insects, in which case his client is defeated. In this country, it is the client, and not the lawyer, who puts his foot into it.

This new attempt to preserve peace had not, however, produced any effect on the mind of the Sultan, anil Admiral Roussin from that moment had not appeared at the Palace of the Porte. THE CHURCIl OF ROME HAS NO , BIBLE WITHOUT NOTES. The following extract from a speecli lately made by the Rev. Hugh M'Neile may not he unacceptable to our readers. It conveys some very important information: " It is not. 1 think, fully and entirely understood that the Romanists have no version of the Bible without notes. It is not understood that their Douay version of the Old, and the Rhemish transalation of the New Testament were mainly concocted by a certain Doctor, named Allen, the founder of the College at Douav and Rheims, and the chief translator of the Rhemish Testament was Dr. Wm Allen. He was an Englishman, but for multiplied acts of treason was compelled to fly from his country. (I quote from Strype' s Annals.) þÿ He went to Flanders, where he exercised ail the powers of his mind þÿ and they were great, to check and, if possible, to overthrow the progress of the Reformation in England. He came a pensioner of the King of Spain, a nd w as created a Cardinal bv the Pope. He laboured to corrupt the soldiery of England, and succeeded in tempting Sir Wm. Stanley to betray Davonter, in Holland, to the Spaniards In concert with the Jesuit Parsons, he devised the scheme oi the Spanish invasion of England in tiie celebrated 'invincible Armada.' fie was patronised bv the infamous Duke de Guise who with Catherine de Medicis, planned the massacre of tens of thousands of Protestants on St. Bartholomew's day ; and he was the willing instrument of Gregory XIII, who appointed a public thanksgiving

at Rome for the success of the ahove-men tioned slaughter. Cardinal Allen sent Jesuits into England, to taint the principles of the people. The pupils of the colleges he founded were taught all manner of wavg to divide the Protestants in the principles of their religion ; and were themselves bound by an oath of which the following is a copy : þÿ ' I. A B., do acknowledge the ecclesiastical and politi cal power of his Holiness, and the Mother Church of Rome, as the chief head and matron, above all pretended churches throughout the whole earth. And that my zeal shall Be for St. Peter and his successors, as the founders of the true and ancient Catholic faith, against all heretical kings, princes, states, or powers, repugnant in to the same. And although I mat/ pretend, in case of persecution, or otherwise, to be heretically disposed ; yet, in my soul and conscience, I shall h Ip, aid, and succour the Mother Church." þÿ Strype's Annals, vol. 2, part. 0, page -237. That was the produce of the translation of the Douav and Rhemish version, which our Ministers would have put into the schools of this country.

" the ambassador of france at constantinople to the president of the council. " Therapia, July 8. This doubt is, however, removed in the next. "the consul general of france at alexandria to the president of the council. " .llexandrm, July 6. " The Egyptians under the order of Ibrahim, having attacked the Turkish army, oommauded liy the Seraskier llafis Pacha, at llezib,, beyond Aleppo, the latter abandoned the held of battle after a combat of two hours. Ibrahim wrote the above on the 25th of June, and in the tent of the Turkish General in Chief He had returned to Antab on the 2Sih. hut had ordered three regiments of infantry and three of cavalry to advance on Oi fa and Di irbekir.1' This news produced little effect on the Paris Bouise, as each interpreted it to his own taste; but in tbe best informed quarters it was stated that Mehemet Ali would declare himself independent.

Letters from Constantinople of the 3d instant have reached us. The intelligence ot the defeat of the Turkish aunt iti Syrin had not reached the Porte when the advices quitted that city. The funeral of the Sultan lias taken place, and nothing could equal the grief One 750 þÿ by the multitude evinced as the cortege passed thro' the cit\ to the place of interment. On his return to the palace the young Sultan appointed his ministry and the officers of his household. 1 he post of Grand Vizier had devolved on Husrew Pasha, the two sons in-law of Mahmoud obtained two important departments, and the Miriistrv of Foreign Affairs, left ad interim to Nourri Effendi. would, it was thought, be coafeiredon Redschid Pacha. On the 2d the European physicians who had attended the Sultan during his last illness were dismissed, I and Dr. Millingen was chosen by his present Highness to be his court physician.

We have received the Parts journals of Saturday and Sunday. The sugar question seems to be the engrossing political topic in France. Yesterday a scene occurred in the Chamber of Deputies, perhaps unparalleled in the histoty of a parliamentary or constitutional government. M. Dulaure, tbe Minister id

Commerce, whose business it is to attend to all the commercial interests of the country, very properly espoused in the Chamber yesterday the cause of the colonists, and intresited the house to reconsider its former verdict. He pleaded that the Sugar Hill should be discussed this þÿsession and he threatened, should the Chamber refuse this act of justice, to resort to the power vested in the government bv the law of IS 14, and to diminish the duty on colonial sugar by ordinance. Gridaine, Duchatel, Teste, and Schneider, actually voted against the Minister of Commerce, and in favour of the adjournment of the law ! By this adjournment of the Sugar Bill the colonies will he ruined, unless the m nisters shall resort to the law of 1314, and make Orders of Council. P vKIS, July 29. Un the 14th instant, the Emperor of Russia published a manifesto on the occasion of the marriage of his daughter with the Duke of Leuchtenberg, in which, after announcing this event to his subjects, he states that it was his intention that their Imperirl Highnesses should fix their residence in Russia, and that, yielding to his affection for his beloved daughter, and to give a r.ew testimony of esteem to the Duke of Leuchtenberg for his distinguished merit, he had thought proper to confer on him the title ot Imperial Highness. PARIS, July 30. News from I lie East. A letter from Alexandria of the 6th July states that the English squadron was expected there every moment. The news from Alexandria is of the 14th of July. The dispatches stated, that an envoy of the Grand Seignor had arrived at Alexandria demanding that the past be forgotten, and that good relations should be established between the two governments. The ' Augsburgh Gazette' gives a letter from Constantinople, of the 9th inst., stating that the llaflz Pacha had been able to rally 25,000 of the Turkish army at Alalatia, whence he was to march again towards the Euphrates. 'This account repeats the rumors that the Capitan Pacha had entered into an

agreement with Ibrahim Pacha, who was to march upon Constantinople, whilst he himself should appear in the Bosphorus, in order to free the young Sultan from the constraint of his present advisers ; and that a s;reat number of executions had taken place in Constantinople.

There is little political news in the Paris journals of Tuesday. The Journal den l)e bats announces that the Bank of England has come to an arrangement with certain Parisian bankers to borrow of the Bank of France two millions sterling on the security of the funds of the English government. þÿ It says : þÿ " For some days past Messrs. Curtis and Baring have occupied themselves in Paris for the Bank of England with a convention to modify the cou rse of exchange, of which the prices were cakilatcd to favour the export of the precious metals in London, and which threatened to exhaust the gold in reserve at the Bank of England, and thus originate a serious commercial crisis. After some explanations the treaty has been definitively concluded, with the co-operation and under the auspices of the Bank of France. Several principal Parisian banking houses have engaged to accept the Bank of England bills for a sum of fifty millions of francs (two millions sterling). The Bank of Fiance will open at these houses a special credit, and w ill discount these bills. For the guarantee of the French capitalists and of the Bank of France the Bank of England will deposit at the latter equal security, consisting of the public luiuis of the English government. This intervention ol French capitalists in the affairs of Great Britain and this support given by the Hank ot France to the Hank of England, are

not only acts dictated by honourable international feeling, but are measures at the same time of wisdom and of great foresight in favour of French industry, for there is an intimate connection between English and French commerce, and the one cannot prosper il the other is shaking ; and any event which would affect the Hank of England would have a terrible counteraction this side of the channel. The Commerce affirms that the negociation alluded to above was not terminated on Monday, and that, at all events, the English government security would not be deposited at the Bank of France, as it is known this establishment can only advance money on French funds. Our private letters, on the other handf state that no doubt existed on the Bourse on Tuesday that the negociation had been definitively concluded. The funds rose in consequence of this belief, added to the fact that the three days had passed off w ithout disturbances, and to the conviction that, in despite of the treason of the Capitan Pacha the Eastern question would be amicably settled. The Times Parisian Correspondent writes: " The accounts brought bv the British steamer Blazer, from Alexandria to Marseilles have not met the public eye ; but this much I have learned (1 trust correctlv), that although Mehemet Ali accepted the offer of the Capitan Pasha to place the Turkish fleet under his protection, he will deliver it up to the Sultan immediately on the conclusion of the definitive treaty understood to be in pro-
gress between thein, through 'he medium of the great powers, France and England in particular."

Tiie intelligence which we announced some days since, received from Colonel Siiiel, and dated from Erzeroom, of the entrance of the Anglo Indian army into Candahar, is fully confirmed by dispatches received yesterday. The army entered Candahar on the 2lst of April. They were most favourably received, and the dhticulties with which they had to contend on tneir march had ent relv disappeared. Private intelligence," says an evening contemporary, " from Candahar to April 29, reports that Shah Shooja had been crowned with acclamation, all the chiefs, with the exception of the Bauckzve Brothers, having signified their adherence to him. Dost Mahomed, it is said, had sent his family to Bokhara. The British army was to proceed forthwith to Cabool, which it is expected to reach in 22 days. " This gratifying intelligence had been received at Peshawur with great rejoicings. The City was illuminated for three days, and preparations were made for the immediate advance of the contingent atmy of Runjeet Sing, accompanied by the Shahzadah Tinioor and Colonel Wade, upon Cabool."

" C,anion, April 7. "Strange events have taken place here. A commissioner has arrived from Pekin to put an end to the opium trade. He commenced taking into custody all the resident, merchants and placing restrictions on their and other factories; also Captain Elliott; declaring that tie would detain them till all the opium was delivered up He would not allow them food or water for some time. Things went on in this way a tew days, when Captain Elliott required all the merchants to deliver up their opium, he guaranteeing payment for the same ; 20.000 chests were given up, and report states that opium ev<m to i he extent of 2,000,000 (pounds sterling or dollars is not given in the letter) was surrounded " Another letter has been received, stating that Captain Elliott and the merchants had be ii r cased, but that all the opium was detamed T >e news produced a rise in the prices of teas on ' Change yesterday afternoon, as s vi al of the British ships had left Canton in bd ist. Lin, a high officer of the Chinese empire, uow s pecialiy appointed an imperial envoy, a president of the board ol war. and viceroy of Hoo Kwang, hereby proclaims to the foreigners of every nation, that they may thoroughly known and understand. Whereas ye, the said foreigners, coming to Canton to trade, hove usually reaped immense profits ; therefore it is that your ships which, in former years amounted annually to no more than several tons, now exceed a hundred and several tons, which arrie here every year. Your import goods, no matter wh it they be. with us find a consumption: and respecting the cargo which you may wish to purchase in return, there is nothing in which you may not adventure. 1 would like to ask you if in the wide earth under heaven you can find such another profit yielding market ns this is I Our great Chinese emperor v ews all mankind with e<uall benevolence, and therefore it is that he has thus graciously permitted you to trade, and become as it were, 9teeped to the lips in gain. For many years the Catholic religion in England, was an object of persecution by slowly but effectually acting laws, tending to paralyse its energies, rath r than to completely deprive it of life That period is now past, and I trust, and flatter myself, that the remembrance of it, as far ns any feeling of resentment is concerned is as completely blotted Out from the hearts of Catholics as the statutes themselves are from the code of England þÿ lint unfortunately, since another method of at- 1 in tack has been pursued, more open, more clamorous, and more directed to wound our feelings, and not onlv so. but much more calculated to ruin the cause of all religion. I allude to that system o! violent declamation, invective and calumny against us, in which so many, who call themselves the followers of th gospel, indulge throughout this country. It has even been the custom to send round men from town to town ; and were it for no other purpose, than merely to preach their own doctrines in their own places of worship, tve could not complain ; not even if they went so iar as to warn their hearers against what they conceived to be erroneous. But to make religion a matter of declamation þÿ to collect Crowds ot men in places usually appropriated to prophane purposes, and to think it a most important duty to break, il possible, in sunder the bonds of social community, of aflection At kindness, which exist among members of different religions, must be blighting to the holiest virtues, and consequently p, t f ic interests

of all Christianity. It is only by the general feeling of society being declared against such a system, that it can possibly be checked and prevented. The following description gives a frightful picture of tins silvery orb of þÿnight.: þÿ þÿ i he character of the entile surface of this moon, so iar as telescope power has made it known to us, is just what might have been expected m a world deprived of air and water and of the tribe of being to whose life tiiese are necessary. This most inhospitable planet exiiimts a wide waste ol surface, diversified by nothing but its lofty mountains and cavernous valleys. Chains of mountains and insulated lulls are spread over every part of the surface, and lift their menacing and precipitous sides frequently to the height of five perpendicular miles. þÿ in many places huge masses of earth spring directly from the plain and carry their peaked summits to the altitude of 20,000 icet. Nor is the extent of the bases of these stupendous eminences less astounding than their heights. The diameters of the bases of several detached lulls of this kind, which measure live miles in height, vary fiom Ci to 4ti miles. þÿ But Uie circumstance which deprives the þÿmoon s surtace ol every trace ol analogy wuh tn.it of tiie earth is tlie enormous circular cavities winch are found in almost every part of a. w une <>i these caverns are four miles depth and 40 miles in diametei. Their edge s generally defended by a high natural wail, frequently a conical mountain rises to a considerable height from the bottom ol this dark circular hole. The top ot this cone is rendered visible when the ruvs ot the sun fail diiuctly into the cavern. This internal

conical uiuun am has sometimes a circular cavity in its apex, like the crater ot the volcano. þÿ The provision which gives to the several planets the grateful returns of the seasons is denied to the moon, and accordingly not a trace can be discovered on her surface of the j slightest variation which can be ascribed to change of season. If, then, the moon be the habitation of living things, they must tic constituted with functions very diflerent from those which characterise the animal and the vegetable kingdoms of the earth. Speech and hearing would therefore be useless (acuities. þÿ No azure tirmamcnl oilers its mild tint to the eyes ol the Selenite. The blue ot our sky is the proper colour of our atmosphere. In the absence of an atmosphere the firmament of the moon is one eternal and unvaried black, through which the glowing orb of the sun holds its solitary way, vainly endeavouring to dil- (use brightness beyond the edge of his own disc. From the New York Commercial Advertiser > July 31, 1839. Correspondence of Commercial Advertiser. London, July 9, 1839 þÿ evening. Tomorrow morning the British Queen departs for New York, with a goodly number of passengers. I was on board this queen of the seas vesterdav, at her anchorage at Black Wall, some four miles from the Bank of Bugland. She is too laige to enter into any of the docks, except that belonging to the Bast India Company, which is rather below Black Wall. When I first saw the Great Western 1 did think she was quite large enough for any navigation, and that it would be a long time before we should see a rival. We have in the Queen, however, a comparison with the former, somewhat like that of a ship of the line with a frigate. 1 am quite satisfied with the Western, and with all lu-r internal arrangements. þÿ She is a tried boat, and fully answers all expectation. 1 hope the Queen will meet all your anticipations, and that there will be passengers enough to remunerate her enterprising owners. Her cabin is beautifully fitted up, and very conveniently arranged. The tables are numerous, and there is sufficient room between them to allow the waiters to pass around without incommoding any one. Her tonnage is 20 Hi tons ; engine 500 horse power 1 þÿ with Hall's condensers. Her length is 275 feet over all. Her beam 03 feet, including guirds; and her depth of hold 29 feet- She w ill draw at her departure from port 16 feet. When she came round from Liverpool, she had, including coal, a freight of fourteen hundred tons. She has now on board six

hundred tons of coal þÿ estimated for twenty days full steaming. The diameter of the cylinder is 77 inches, with a seven feet stroke. She will carry more canvass than the Great Western ; and will probably sail faster without the aid of steam. Her speed can be better judged of bv you after she has made a trip. The greatest speed of the Western, when we came out, w as thirteen and a half miles per hour. This was only made a few hours on the last day we were at sea. It appears that we are to have still larger ships than the Queen. The Great Western steam ship company are preparing to build an iron steamer, to run in connection with their present ship. She is to be named the " M B W Y OliK," and will have engines of one thousand horse j/ower. The Steam Navigation Company has another ship to be added to the British Queen. She is in a state of great forwardness, and will be called the " PRESIDENT." She will probably bo ready for sea early next spring. I have examined her thoroughly ; and I assure you, she is as strong as wood, iron and copper can make her. Her extreme length, over all, will be 270 þÿfeet on deck 215; her deck 41 feet wide, not including her þÿguards -depth 27 J feet; and she will draw 17 feet. She will carrv GOO tons of freight, and the same quantity of coal. Her flooring is of solid oak, with five kelsons, four of which are double and very large. Every piece of timber is secured by iron braces at an angle of forty five degrees, and also with wooden trusses. Her engines, of
five hundred and twenty horse power, arc

SAXTSR TSSJriSTSaSIK ma&iaRlSTOS AT23 building at Liverpool. This noble vessel, when ready for sea, will have cost eighty thousand pounds sterling. The British Queen, I am told, is the longest vessel ever built. It is rather singular that the engines are made at one part ol the kingdom and the ship at another. The Great Western was built at Bristol, and came round to London, to take in her engines. The Queen was built in London and her engines at Liverpool. The tonnage ot the latter will be over 2000 tons. 1 was at the House of Lords to hear the great debate on Friday, on the motion of the primate, in retion to national education. 1 refer you to the Saturday's paper for a full report of the proceedings on that most interesting occasion The Lords go up on Thursday to the palace, in a body, to present the address to her Majesty. In the Commons, on the same day, the proceedings were interesting. The budget was presented, and you will see that in consequence ot the Canadian troubles, there is a tery considerable deficiency. Saturday was to nte a day of uncommon interest. 1 heard Lord Brougham speak for more than an hour, and Mr. O'Connell for about the same time. 1 suppose they may be considered the two best orators of the present dav in Bngland. It was a rich repast, and would have been more " so had it not been for the repeated cry of hear, hear, hear," and " bravo, bravo bravo." with thundering clapping. There were many other speakers, but it was of little use lor any one to attempt speaking after such men as these.

When audiences want to put a stop to a long winded speaker, they compel him to withdraw by a continual noise with the feet, and the cry of "time, time, time." The occasion that called out Lord Brougham and Mr. O'Connell was the formation of a society for the relief of British India, which will probably lead to important changes in the government of that vast country. 1 refer you to the papers of yesterday for the report of the proceedings. If you have not room for them entire, perhaps you may be able to crowd iu a briel sketch. Wednesday Morning, July 10. You will see by the accounts from Birmingham, that the Giiartists are still very troublesome. You will perhaps remember that a party of gentlemen left London last year, in a balloon of large dimensions, and alter an unprecedented journey, landed at Nassau, in Germany. This travelling vehicle known as the Royal " JS'assau " On is now Monday it was again sent up from Vuuxhall, with seven gentlemen attached to it, viz: Messrs. Green, Sir G. Kent, Duff, Fielding, Wellesley, Corrie and Hughes. They took their departure from the garden at 20 minutes after G o'clock, and landed at Toppersfield at half post 8 o'clock, a distance of 53 miles. 1 had a fine view of the scene from the Commercial Road, on my way from the British Queen. The balloon was then over Stepney Church, and remained, apparently stationary, for many minutes. A great meeting of the dissenters of this country is to be bold at Durslcv, in Gloucestershire, on the 30th instant, to be called

the White field Centenary Commemoration. Dr. Ration of New York is to be present. This morning, a little after 5 o'clock, the funeral procession of the lamented Lady Flora Hastings passed in sight from my wiu-

dows. It was an imposing spectacle, and brought very painful associations to my mind, on reflecting npon some events con. nected with her death, which had been communicated to me by one who was acquainted with the melancholy case. The procession, when it passed Cheapside, consisted of some forty carriages. The hearse was drawn by six large black horses, covered with black« with plumes and escutcheons The mourning coaches followed, drawn each by six horses. The royal carriages the same, and the pageant closed with the private carriages of noblemen and gentry, all completely shut up. A large number of the Queen's servants were in attendance. 1 have seen her majesty the Queen, three or four times during my short sojourn in this capital, and although I have not yet been admitted to a private audience, 1 have been near enough to her royal person to hear her converse. 1 cannot think that she is beautiful or even pretty, but there is something very interesting in her appearance þÿ perhaps it was the circumstances under which 1 saw her ; first coming out of Buckingham House þÿ then on Constitution Hill and two or three times in Hyde Bark, surrounded bv thousands. She appears two or three years younger than she is þÿ I think a stranger would suppose her from 1G to 17. Her dress was at all times very plain þÿ a riding habit of bottle green, not so long as those we see in New York, a plain black riding hat, with a black veil, light blue handkerchief tied around the neck, with the
hair very plain. Although yon see her represented in her robes in the prints in New- York, 1 am informed that she generally dresses very simply. «»»»<»

the paris barricades. (From Fr user's Magazine.) " Did you ever, my dear Eraser, see a barricade? Perhaps not. Then do let me give you a description. First ot all imagine a hundred fellows, some short and others tall, some ferocious, and others athletic, politely threatening to take away the lives of all the inhabitants of half-a-dozen houses in the next tive minutes, if they make the least resistance to the formation of a barricade in front of their dwellings. Then imagine 300 fellows seizing hold of iron bars, or spades, or crows, or whatever is the strongest and most handy, to tear up the paving stones ; and the male inhabitants of the houses afoiosaid compelled to aid in this work of preparation. Then the paving stones are piled one on the other. Spades and shovels ure used to dig a trench. The earth is thrown up. Planks, chests of drawers, ladders, poles, weighty and cumbrous articles are all heaped together; and ' confusion worse confounded" is the order of the day. Behind these rapidly collected and arranged materials, the rebels charge their muskets; and as no cavalry can pass, they have only to fear the infantry, who are armed like themselves. In the houses adjoining, at the first, second, and third lloois, are planted rebel sentinels, who utter cries or make signs when the enemy is approaching. Up and down the street, at all the windows, you see a hundred caps and bonnetts. The women love a barricade, enjoy the fun of an erneule, rejoice at an insurrection, triumph at

rebellion; arid in Paris a favourite pastime for the fair and biave Parisian females, is to watch who takes the best aim, and shoots his brother or his neighbour with the most dexterity. C'est bien , e'est bien I" cried an old woman of 00. when, from behind a barricade Rue Neuve St. Mery, a young beardless rebel of 18 levelled his gun, and shot a captain of infantry dead on the spot. The soldiers looked up scornfully. The old woman repeated the cry. " C'est bien, c'est bien !" she screamed. But she never uttered another word, for the soldiers became angry as well as scornful þÿ pointed their muskets, and she was dead. This was the signal for new barricades, and new disorders."

It is impossible to read this dispatch without feeling deeply affected by the prominent manner in which the providence of God has shown itself on this, as on many other occasions, with reference to Turkish affairs. Prophecy must be accomplished. The days of the Turkish empire are numbered. All deplomatic attempts to prop it up, though honestly meant, must tail against the positive declarations of the Word of God. Worldly wisdom boasted much of the talents of Mahmoud, of the reforms he had accomplished, and was still destined to perform. The French Infidels and the German Geologists lauded him to the skies. He undertook to reduce the l'acha of Egypt to submission. He piomiscd the Divan that he would soon repossess Syria þÿ and already, those who have no belief in the providence of God, and who are indifferent to his revealed Word, proclaimed that the Pacha must fall, and the glory of Mohammedanism would re-appear. But whilst man. in Ins blindness and his ignorance proposes, God it is who disposes þÿ and at the very moment when the Turks and the Divan were expecting to hear of the progress ol' Turkish arms, and the defeat of the Egyptian usurper, the hand of death is pla-

þÿ þÿin .g.i.a.iwtvnn ced on the heart of Mahmond þÿ and this mighty reformer is no more. So true it is that God makes use of even such instruments as Mehemet Ali and Ibrahim Pacha to subserve his all-wise and all glorious designs, and to accomplish those prophecies, every word of which must be fulfilled to the very letter. Mohammedanism, like Popery, most be overthrown, and the Christian readers of a Conservative Protestant journal like the St. James s Chronicle will require no apology from me for reminding them, that Christian Protestant Conservatives ought not to allow such events as the one which has just occurred to transpire, without proclaiming that Christianity is at the root of all these fluctuations, and that the promises of God, as well as his threatenings, must and will be fulfilled. The eldest son of the Sultan is a weakminded, as well as sickly, young man of 17. His reign will probably be most short ; at any rate it will be feeble and disastrous to the Ottoman Porte. At a moment like the present, when it has lost the only man ot nerve and resolution þÿ when Mahmoud is dead þÿ when Ibrahim and Mehemet will be rampant with and full of the most ambitious projects what can the new Sultan do- -the þÿ soft, effeminate late, beardless boy of 17 ? His brothers in law will be his rivals, the enemies of Mahmoud will be his foes ; and it is by no means impossible that some cabal may terminate his days. Sultan Mahmoud Khan II. was horn 14th Ramazan, 1 199, of the Ottoman awn, or 20th of July, 1785, of the Christian calender.

A report has been received from the gentlemen who have formed the deputation lrom this town on the subject of the contemplated change in this important department of the public service, which our readers will perceive, from the subjoined extracts, is decisive of the intention of the government. We have marked two or three passages in italics which particularly merit the attention of the public. The Chancellor of the Exchequer stated that " parties had offered to contract with government on a large scale" for the conveyance of the mails by steam, and that government " were obliged to listen to such an offer ; and tiie public would insist on it." þÿ Mr. Wood, at the Admiralty, stated that þÿ "the proposals made were so favourable, that they could not be competed with ; that the country would expect such an offer would be embraced ; and it was not the intention of the government to advertise foj tenders." Of these two gentlemen, we may say, with Dogberry, " Fore Gad, they are both in a tale I" But we are greatly in error if the information they have thought proper to give on this subject will be deemed sufficient to satisfy the public ; and if their present intention be pertinaciously persevered in, we hope they will be required by Parliament to give some explanation of this unprecedented mode of procedure. That they should suddenly break up the Sailing- Packet Establishment þÿ destroy a populous town and neighbourhood
þÿ injure to a great extent a whole county-

introduce a new system for the conveyance of the mails, which will necessarily involve the country in an expenditure of at least £500,000 per þÿannum enter upon a contract for years to come and grant a charter of þÿ monopoly to a company of stock-brokers ; arid all this without consulting Parliament þÿ without a complaint from the great mercantile interests of the kingdom against the existing mode of conveyance þÿ without advertising for lenders to throw it into open competition, or communicating their design to any one, until it was reluctantly dragged from them by the deputation, does appear to us, and must to the country, a most extraordinary, not to say a suspicious, course of measures. How can Mr. Rice presume that "the public would insist" on this plan without its being made known to them ? How can Mr. Wood venture to assert, until results of a public advertisement were known, that " the proposals were so favourable that they could not be competed with ?" Favourable? To whom ? If to the contractors, it will be naturally and reasonably a«k»d, why any favoured company of stock-jobbers should be elected by the government to dip their hands exclusively in the pockets of the people, and drain tliern to such an enormous amount ? ft may be asked by what means are Mr. Rice & Mr Wood enabled to see so clearly the advantages which the public will derive from this covert contract? and improved their vision. Mr. Wood stated his ' readiness to answer any inquiry that might be put, and show why they accepted the private proposals, and did not ask for tenders." Curious clock. þÿ The most curious thing in the cathedral of Lubeck is a clock of singular construction, and very high antiquity. Jt is calculated to answer astronomical purposes, representing the places of the sun and moon in the ecliptic, the moon's age, a perpetual almanac, and many other contrivances. The clock, as an inscription set forth, was placed in the church on Candlemas day in 1405. Over the face of it appears an image of our Saviour, and on either side of the image are folding doors, so constructed as to fly open cveiy day when the clock strikes twelve. At this hour, a set of figures representing the twelve apostles come out from the door on the left hand of the image, and pass bv in review before it, each figure making its obeisance by bowing as it passes that ol our Saviour, and afterwards entering the door on the right hand. When the procession terminates, the doors close. þÿ Clarke's Travels in Scandinavia.

Tiie Affvirs of the East. þÿ The late interesting news from Turkey leaves in considerable uncertainty and doubt the state of the affairs of the empire. In relation to the advances which have been made to the wily and powerful viceroy of Egypt there is a good deal of contradiction, and independently of this many of the stories seem extremely improbable. It is however, impossible, in the present state of information, to establish any plausible theory for explaining the state of things. We give some of the icports and speculations from the English and French papers. From the London Morning; Chronicle, July 31. The Turkish and Egyptian War þÿ The Moniteur of Friday contained the following telegraphic despatch Irom Marseilles ot the events of the 25th : " The death of the Sultan was known at Alexandria on the 8th ; and on the following day a Turkish schooner reached Alexandria with Negib Bey, kiaya of the Capitan Pacha, on board, charged to i It would not surprise us much to hear, announce to the Viceroy of Egypt the presence of the Capitan Pacha at Slankio. on his way to Rhodes, and to propose to place the Turkish fleet under the Viceroy's protection, in order to guard against the troubles likely to follow the Sultan's death in Turkey. A reply was despatched by Mehemct Ali. in the steam boat called the Black Sea. to the Capitan Pacha ; hut its tenor is unknown. On the 10th Askiff Effendi, sent by the Sultan to announce the death of his father, reached Alexandria." This corroboration of the defection of the

Turkish Admiral with the fleet is had enough. But worse ami still more startling O tidings O have, we fear, to be added to it. These are, that the members of the new Divan, or government, at Constantinople, have taken a step similar to that of the Capitan Pacha, and have written to Mehemet Ali to put themselves and the Sultan under his protection, offering him the hereditary government of Syria and Egypt, and inviting Mehemet Ali to Constantinople to reorganise the government. A knowledge of the Capitan Pacha's defection of an insurrection prepared at Constan- þÿ tinople as well as in Albania is said to have þÿ decided Ivhosrew and Haiti to this surrender of the empire and of their young Sovereign. Their own disagreement, their want of mutual confidence, and the complete inexperience of Abdul Dedjid, are the motives which led these ministers to submit to the Egyptian I'acha, by a simultaneous, but, it appears, by no joint step. Serious, however, as this event must appear, it loses much of its gravity from the impossibility any of such result being accomplished as that contemplated by the defectionists. England, France, and Austria are not rendered the less resolute by these intrigues, to maintain the independence of the Ottoman empire. Nor can either Mehemet or the Divan act in despite of them. It is not, indeed, probable that Mehemet would wish to risk the enmity of all the world, for scarcely less would be the consequence of his entering Constantinople. It may be thought, that if

the intrigues and gold of Mehemet have prepared the defection of the licet, with troubles hi Constantinople and in Albania, Russian counsels may have prompted the Divan to fling itself headlong into the arms of Mehemct, iu order to afford a pretext lor Russian inter-

ference. This we do not think. Russia is not prepared for so hold a cast ot the die ; and, if she were so. never were the other European powers better prepared or more resolved to prevent Russia carrying oil tlie prize. The Boris Journal des Dehats offers the following reasoning upon the present aspect of affairs at Alexandria: þÿ The Messager of Saturday evening contains the following: þÿ "If our informant be correct, as we have every reason to believe, Mehemet Ali has accepted the proposal of Ahmed Ferezi. the Capiian l'acha, and had taken the Turkish fleet under his protection. » It would also appear than an envoy from Abdul Medjid had been sent, not only to confer upon the viceroy the hereditary title to Egypt, hut also the office of commander-inchief of the laud and sea lorces, with an invitation to come to Constantinople for the purpose ot consulting upon matters of great state interest." The above news, although seemingly prcmature. lias, however, a claim to probability. in the course of a few days, that Mchemct Ali had embarked on board the Admiral s ship, and proceeded to Constantinople with the Ottoman fleet, in order to pay homage lo the new Sultan, and oiler his long experience and sorvices to the young padischa. Thus, by a complete change of system with respect to Egypt, the Ottoman policy would adopt the new course which we wished lor» and developed in two former þÿarticles namely, the union ol the Turkish power and the Egyptian power, with the view of emanci-

pating Turkey from die Russian protectorate, as well as from European jealousies, which serve to keep alive a spirit ol discord bciweeu the two Mussulman states. Giving merely its just value to the expression, Arabian nationality, of which so much has been said, and taking into account the exact state of the political establishment of the viceroy of Egypt, it cannot he denied that this establishment rallies to the same centre of power the Mussulman population of Arabian race and language. This is what forms the future prospects of this system, and makes the most incredulous admit that we are at present contemplating a great historical laot þÿ namely, the Inundation ol a new empire. On the other hand the Mussulman's of the Turkish race and language have the centre of their power at Constantinople, and it is worthy of remark that amongst all the provinces which the empire has lost þÿ for instance, Wallachia, Georgia, Scrvia and Greece, there is not a single Turkish province, whilst she has preserved infaot all those in which the pure Ottoman race had established their homes. By glancing at the map it will he easily perceived that Turkey is still as extensive as all þÿAustria Turkey is still strong and capable of self-preservation. The brilliant step which Mehemet Ali is about to take, his presence at Constantinople, his great reputation ; and the advice which he will give, cannot fail to save the Turkish empire from the frightful anarchy into which it was on the point of being precipitated by

the defeat of the Turkish army and the desertion of the fleet, l'eacc, a certain and lastfluence. The powers ing one, will be the result ol Ins personal is lo whose interest it insec Turkey and Egypt destroy each other, will endeavour to prevent the conclusion ol

a treaty by alleging, as a pretext, their attachment to the integrity of Turkey ; but their efforts will bo in vain, in opposition to the voice of the Mussulman population, who may replv, " l.et us agree among ourselves; the towns and provinces of which we dispose are not Christian þÿ they are not frontier places belonging to any European possession þÿ let us therefore settle our own affairs." Finally, the wish of Mehemet Ali has lieen long known ; he asks nor wants no more ; and he is well aware that, if he carried his ambition bevond the Arabian districts, the opinion of the Turkish people would be turned against him. This result ought to cause general satisfaction, as its unforeseen and irresistable effect must be to crush secret ambition and thwart those desires and machinations which would have made the eastern question the grounds of a general war. 1'cace is now certain, and we anxiously await the accomplishment of the wishes wc have so often expressed on this subject.

Pursuant to notice, one of the largest and most respectable meetings of shipmasters ever assembled in this city, met on Thursday evening, at the Second W ard Hotel, lot the purpose of consultation, and of taking further measures in reference to Consul I rist, and the shipmasters and seamen abandoned and oppressed by the said consul, at Havana. Captain Edward Rossi ter w as called to the Chair; Captains J. Hillman, Henry Russell, and James W. Low, were appointed Vice- Presidents ; and Captains S. E. Glover and B. Ritchie were appointed Secretaries.

The objects of the meeting being slated by the President, Captain Rossiter, the following preamble and resolutions were offered by Capt. S. E. Glover : Whereas, it is the bounden duty of every United States ministerial or consular agent abroad, anil especially the peculiar province of consuls and consular agents, vigilantly to watch over and carefully to protect and guard the interest of American commerce and seamen from foreigu aggression, as well as to prevent harsh treatment of crews by shipmasters, and to put down and punish mutinous insurrections, or other difficulties occurring on board of all vessels in foreign ports : And whereas, such authentic facts have been presented to this meeting as prove conclusively that Nicholas U. Trist, the consul at Havana, has been guilty of secretly inciting the Spanish authorities to the unlawful condemnation and imprisonment of American captains and seamen for alleged and unfounded off-nces produced by him against them ; and, when remonstrances were presented to the said Trist against his high-handed conduct, by one hundred and Jlfty live respectable shipmasters and citizens of Havana, comprising nearly all that reside there, and that the said remonstrance, when laid before hint by Commander Babbit. of tiie United States sloop of war Boston, then in port, he, the said consul, treated the same with contemptuous scorn, and so misrepresented lus proceedings, as fully to establish, by his own admissions the truth of his accusations against him There-

fore be it. Resolved, as the sense of this meeting, 'That the conduct of the said Trist has been wanton, tyrannical, unlawful, and unjust, arul highly injurious and offensive to our profession. Resolved, That the proceeding of the said Consul, tu ettcoui aging the Spanish authori-

ties to bring to unlawful trial, on ex: jr"-vat« 4 charges, the crew ol the American ship " William hngs," and causing tlum to he condemned without counsel or trial by jury, and sentenced like common felons, to chairs and hard labor, in breaking stones iitidor Spanish task masters, is enough to stamp the name of 7'rist wiih infamy, and to prove him totally unworthy to hold his high and, what ought to he, honorable station. Resolved, That the tyrannical, illegal, and unjust imprisonment of Captain Abraham Wendell, jr., of the brig Kremlin, of this port, during a protracted period ot five months, and his continuance under bonds for an additional period of three months, on the false accusations brought by said Trist against Captain Wendell in the Spanish Courts, and which lie failed in any instance to sustain, is anoihcr evidence of the tyranical and malignant spirit of persecution which has constantly marked the conduct of said Trist towards his countrymen. Resolved , 'That in our opinion, the fetter which lias been subsequently written by said 7'rist, and recently published in the New Orleans Courier, and subsequently in the Globe and other papers, concerning the interference of Commander Babbit, ana in which letter, he, the said 7'rist, denounces his accusers, meaning thereby all Americans in Havana, as a " set of the vilest and most notorious wretches," as" dirty sneaking knaves," and " characters of the deepest infamy," is by the gross and billingsgate epithett it employs

corrobative proofs of the turpitude of his ow n character, and conclusive evidence that he is unfit for the dignified office he disgraces, as he is destitute of the feelings of an Ameiican, and unworthy the name of a gentleman. Resolved, 7'hat the confession made by him in the said letter, that lie had been convinced that the Capt. of the "Win. Engs" should have been made to break stones in place ol' his guilt in forcing that crew to prison through the agency of the Spanish tribunals þÿ showing also, when too late, a mean attempt at subterfuge, and to win over at the expense of a base and unfounded aspersion upon the Captain þÿ the good opinion of the crew upon whom he had been instrumental in the commission of a most flagrant outrage. Resolved, That the calumnious insinuations thrown out in the aforesaid letter of the said Trist upon the American ship masters and residents of Havana, that he could have bought tbeir good opinion with dinners and other courtesies, is worthy of the author who uttered it, as no other individual but one possessing Ins hostile feelings towards his countrymen, could have measured the integrity and independence of American citizens by a standard so sordid and corruptible. Resolved, 7'hat the great body of Americans, ship masters and citizens of Havana, whose names were attached to the memorial presented to Capt. Babbit, as well as the names of those who attend tins meeting, fling back these reproachlul expressions of Consul 7'rist, and warn lum to clear up his character

first, and especially the charges embraced in the documents printed by the British minister, inculpating the aforesaid Trist, as a participant in the slave trade, before lie has the effrontery to accuse others ot being brined by the courtesies, or any other favor lie can bestow. Resolved, That we respectfully urge upon the seamen and ship masters of every city in lire Union, to co-operate m tire adoption of

such measures as may bring to a speedy recall the aforesaid Nicholas I'. Trist, for his Oppression, illegal and violent outrages upon American citizens, that he may he summoned to trial to atone for conduct which is not only disgraceful to him as an individual, hut is dishonorable to onr country in a foreign land. Resolved, 7'hut a memorial be presented to the proper authorities for the removal of the aforesaid Consul Trist, and that a committee be appointed to prepare and superintend the same: þÿ whereupon the following Captains were appointed upon said committee : Captains Hillman, Knssel, Low, It. E. Glover, Atkins: and Captains 8. E. Glover and Ritchie as secretaries. Resolved, That the unblushing attempt of the said consul to vindicate himself and to challenge his accusers to the proof, while he reiterates offensive epithets upon the bonds of respectable American ship masters and citizens residing in, or trading to Havana, is another additional evidence of the effect of the intoxication of office upon the mind of a person. whose recreant conduct proves him to he by nature prone to acts of the most flagitious description. Resolvd, That in consideration of the extreme severity and harsh treatment received by Captain Wendell, at the hands of the aforesaid 7'rist, and in consequence of the sufferings and privations experienced during his confinement, by a numerous fainilv, consisting of a wile and live daughters, we do cheerfully agree to raise a lurid to sustain Captain

Wendell in a civil suit in the courts of the United States against the said Consul Trist, and we do therefore recommend that subscription papers be opened for this purpose. Resolved. 7'liat the proceedings of the meeting be signed by the President, Vice Presidents and Secretaries of this meeting, and that all the papers in the city he and they are hereby requested to publish the same. SAINT VINCENT. IMPROVEMENTS IN SUGAR BOILING. to the editor. Gibson Hill, Montrose Estate. þÿSir, I take this opportunity of thanking you for the remarks vou made in your paper of the 23rd May, relative to Mr. H. Crosley's Patent Apparatus for Boiling Sugar. As Agent for that Gentleman, I am anxious to explain briefly to the public the principle l of the Apparatus, and in doing so to compare it with the other best known means of acquiring the same end. The advantages of evaporating a solution of Sugar at low temperature has long since been fully proved by the adoption of the Vacuo method of evaporation in Demerara, where, by the use of the Vacuum Pan as a striking teach only, a given quantity ol cane juice has produced a greater weight of crystal vzing Sugar than by any other method ; but with all the advantage of Vacuo method of evaporating, and however ingenious the mode of exhausting the Pan, there still exists several essential drawbacks to its use iu the Sugar Colonies, and although and it its appendages are scientific, yet they are expensive and complicated. It is perhaps not generally known or understood, that the cane juice, when evaporated iu the Vacuum or covered pan, from which the atmospheric influence is excluded, produces crystals of a more glutinous and deliquescent quality than those obtained in an open Fan, in which the influence of the atmosphere is per milted to act in the natural way, or in an open pan into which atmospheric air is propelled or artificially employed in excess,

and that by such last mentioned means the grains or crystals of all sorts of Sugar are pure or hard and not so susceptible to the action oj humidity as Sugar made in any other way. To remedy the defects in the Vacuo method of evaporation at low temperature, is the object intended and now accomplished by Mr. H. Crosley's Apparatus. In the Vacuum Pan not only is the atmosphere excluded (and therefore the Oxygen contained in the atmosphere prevented from exerting its influence on the Sugar), but a great part of the Oxygen that Sugar contains as a natural agent is evaporated by the heat applied and exhausted hv the Pump or other means used for exhausting the air and steam from the Pan. The consequence is that when the sugar is exposed to the atmosphere it again takes up as much of its natural agent again as it had been deprived of, and of course as much water as is combined with that quantity of the Oxygen of the atmosphere. In Mr. It. Crosley's Apparatus this defect cannot take place (in which an excess of the atmospheric air is employed), it may part with the excess ot Oxygen impregnated into it, but will lake up no moisture in consequence. One gruat object in evaporating the cane juice into Sugar, is to prevent carbonization. The application of steam alone at a very high I pressure would do Hus, and on the first stages 1

þÿrwi f' þÿ ' of the operation /that is to say, wht n the Syrup is thin) the evaporation will lie rapid; but in the latter stages, most especially iu the striking teach, the evaporation vvnl l»c far too slow. As the liquid approaches it to pioof it contains but a small quantity of water, and its affinity for heat becomes dimim-hed iu consequence, so much so, that evaporation is barely perceptible. If Sugar exposed is too long even to the action of a low degree of heat, its strength tor crystalization will be greatly impaired. The Vacuum Pan overcomes this difficulty by removing the pressure of the atmosphere from the surface ot the liquid, thereby allowing the almost pent up vapour to rise freely from it. Mr. II. þÿCroslev s Apparatus effects the same object by counteracting the pressure ot the atmosphere, which is done by injecting air at a greater pressure than the pressure ot the atmosphere, and diffusing it by a peculiar method throughout the whole of the liquid undergoing evaporation, and at the same time the whole is kept iu constant circulation so that all parts are equally exposed to the action of the heat and air. Not only is the pressure of the atmosphere counters cted, but the vapour readily combines with the air as it passes into and through the liquid, producing a quicker evaporation than is obtained by the Vacuum Pan, at the same time doing it at a low degree >>l heat and the crystals have not that deliquescent quality. Another essential advantage it possesses is,

that the syrup is exposed to the sight of the operator, enabling turn easily to judge of its progress þÿ while in the Vacuum Pan it is completely covered up, requiring much more skill and attention on his part, and in a manner quite new to him. Coupling these remarks with the facts stated in the Advertisement, 1 think it will be admitted that Mr. H. Crosley's Apparatus is more than as efficient as the Vacuum Pan for manufacturing raw sugar, less complicated, and easier worked ; its cost is not halt so much, nor is it so liable to get out ot þÿorder. i The above observations only relate to the striking teach ; oil another occasion 1 siiult take the liberty io address you on otiier matters connected with it. Your most obedient servant Wm. Manwaking, Engineer.

PARTICULARS OF THE BATTLE OF NK7.IB, I he Turkish army, say the government dispatches from Marseilles, occupied a strong position Nezib. Ibrahim, who had received at the Pacha s permission to make an attack, wished to assail this position in front ; but Soliman Hey (Colonel Selves) succeeded in restraining his ardour, and it was agreed that the enemy should be drawn by manoeuvres from his entrenchments. The Egyptians made a feigned retreat, and the Seraskicr, Haliz Pacha, sent out a strong division of j cavalry. The first corps it came up with, composed of Bedouins, dispersed, according to the orders they had received, and the Seraskier, imagining that the Egyptians might be easily routed, advancing with the whole of his forces. Thus he abandoned his strong position, and two formidable redoubts constructed by Prussian officers, from which great advantage was anticipated. In order to draw the Turks still further from their enti enchmonts, Ibrahim and Soliman continued to retire for two hours, hastening to

gum a field of battle which the superior judg- | ment of Selves had previously selected as one of the most favorable. On reaching this ground the Egyptian army suddenly faced right about, and, availing itself of the nature of the position, formed into compact masses, the infantry in the centre, the cavaliy and light artillery on each wing, and made vigorous charges on the Turks, who were astounded by this sudden attack. The ranks ot the latter were soon thrown into disorder. The Seraskier, however, rode up to the front, and by his valor and the bravery of the corps around him remedied for a time his false step His heavy artillery, unfortunately for him. could not come up, and the light guns ot the Egyptians, directed by European officers, and seconded bv well-timed charges of cavalry, threw his ranks into disorder. Ilis wings were at the same time too extended, and his troops, excited by the aidour ot pursuit, had not preserved anv regular order of battle. They could, thcretorc, scarcely make any resistance, and at this period some corps of Arabs, which Ibrahim in his letreat left in ambush on the right and left, fell upon the Turkish rear, and thus completely put the Ottoman troops to the rout. I he disorder became so great that the I urkish soldiers threw away their arms, and fled in the utmost confusion. Part of the troops endeavoured to regain the entrenched camp, while others made for the most fordable points of the Euphrates. It appears that a large portion ol the fugitives

succeeded in escaping, and that the massacre was not so great as might have been expected. But the camp, artillery, baggage, and even the muskets of the Turkish army, fell into the hands of the Egyptians. The Seraskier carried away in the general rout, crossed the Euphrates. Prodigious masses of people crowded the Battery and the wharves and vessels on the East River, to see these ships go off. The number was þÿlegion and the roofs of the houses were pretty well filled, not only in New York, but in Brooklyn and Jersey City. It is stated by those who had a whole view of this display of the multitude from the roofs of houses in favorable situations, that there has been nothing like it in New York for a long j time. The ladies of that part of the city which overlooks the East River, and the ladies of VV illiamsburgh. Brooklyn &o seemed | to have deserted their parlours and saloons for the roofs of their houses. Brooklyn heights were lined with people. The Steam Boats in the harbour made a most magnificent show as an escort on the occasion. How many of these Boats there were it is difficult to say, for at limes, the East River seemed to be full of them, þÿ but conspicuous among the j number was the Neptune, which, it is said, had eleven hundred persons at the time þÿ Streaming with flags as they were and alive with person, the whole scene presented a picture of uncommon beauty. Anything like an estimate of the number of persons who were viewing this departure of the steam ships would he hut the merest conl jecture, but we are told that the crowd that thronged the Piers, where the Ships were, was immense, þÿ and we very much doubt whether any event in the City of late years, has attracted at once such a multitude of gazers. The curiosity even of the softer sex

so got the better of their timidity, that they, with their children pretty well tilled the piers, and the surrounding wharves where the ships were. Business was for a time suspended, and so much were the population absorbed, that at times parts of the City seemed to he quite deserted. There is but little doubt that these Ships intend to try, the one to beat the other þÿ and the people here have become so much interested, that a large amount in bets is depending upon the result.

ANECDOTE OF A GAME COCK. On tiie memorable 1st of June, (Lord þÿHowe victory.) s Captain Berkeley, the uncle of the present Honorable Grantley Berkeley, commanded the Marlborough, and broke through the French line, LTinpctieux arid Lemuctus each of superior force, and engaged them both. On going into action, the Captain ordered all the live stock to be thrown overboard, but at the humble request of his crew, permitted them to retain an old game cock, which they (the crew) had fought several times and always with success. Though the coob was thrown into the sea, the cock was allowed to range the deck at liberty, la the action, the Marlborough was so severely handled by her tremendous opponents that half her crew were disabled, her Captain carried wounded below, her mainmast shot away, and the remainder of the men driver, from their quarters. At this very juncture, when the Marlborough was on the point of striking, there chanced one of those awful lulls in the rear of the thundering cannon often experienced in general action ; in that momentary silence, when the falling of a rope might be heard, the old game cock, who had escaped the human carnage, hopped up on the shaU tered stump of the mainmast, and with a loud and triumphant flipping of his wings, sent forth such a long and lusty challenge as to lie heard in every part of the disabled ship. .\<» individual spoke in reply to the homely but touching alarm þÿ one universal and gallant cheer from the broken crew arose, they remembered the indomitable courage oi the

bird that sat undismayed above the breeding horrors of the deck, and every soul on board who could drag their limbs to quarters remanned the guns resumed the action, uuj forced each of their opponents to surrender, A silver medal was struck by the order of Admiral Berkeley ; it was hung upon the m k of the old g ime cock, who in the parks n>d around the princely halls of Good wood, pasacd the remainder ol In downy datsw r:d safety.- Rr.Hts.h Nai<if Jiiftoiy,

LIGHT HOUSE. The meeting at. the Town Hall, on Saturdav last, to take into consideration the propriety ol erecting E'l'ht Houses, was well attended bv the merchants and other Gentlemen of the Colony, and, it was unanimously agreed that their erection vonld he greatly conducive to the prevention of the shipwrecks which so frequently occur on the rocks oil our coast. The establishment of Light Houses here, is a subject that has long been mooted ; and the importance of, and the beneficial effects that must result from them, is readily admitted, but, for the want of means, such an establishment has not vet been undertaken þÿ our resources being of too limited a nature to afford a sufficient sum. From the peculiar situation of our islands, vessels are continually passing and re passing, and the extended line ol reels by which we are surrounded, not only rrnder them inaccesable at night time, but even their approach extremely hazardous. Within the last ten years, as appeared by a report from the Collector of H. JV1. Customs, read at the Meeting, thirty-seven vessels were stranded on the rocks off here, four only of that number being bound in þÿ the rest on voyages elsewhere, ami chiefly foreign. 1 or our own trade the benefit of Light Houses will he comparatively trifling, as the Masters of vessels, owned in this colony, are so well acquainted with the dangerous parts of the coast, that injury to our shipping seldom, or never occurs ; hut it is for strangers and foreigners

who have no accurate knowledge ol our po. silion that their establishment is necesscrv. A copy of the proceedings of the Meeting are to he sent to his Excellency the Governor, requesting their transmission to England : and we sincerely hope that when her Majesty s Government may become acquainted with the utility of the measure, immediate steps will be taken to carry it into effect. þÿ July 13.
