From the New York Daily E.rpress. Nov. 15. Naval Force for the coasts of Africa and Bra Slave Trade þÿ Right of Search þÿ American zil þÿ By the arrival at Norfolk of the brig Retrieve, we have accounts of the detention of brtg Two Friends at Santa Cruz, Tenerifie, under suspicion of being engaged in the slave trade. This is the fourth capture of American vessels under like suspicions ; and unfortunately, except in the latter case, without the hitervcntion of United States authority. It is a matter of some surprise that the government here have not sent more of her vessels to accomplish that, which the English cruizers are vigorously carrying on though at the sacrifice of one of our dearest maritime rights þÿ one which was the great cause of our late war with that nation. The right of search formerly contended for, and which was abandoned at the Treaty of Ghent is again virtually assumed b v the course of the British cruizers, and, however we may feel inclined to applaud their zeal and efforts in the suppression of this abominable traffic, we cannot but consider it a dangerous innovation of our rights, and a countenance of precedent which may become more and more dangerous, J o the more we may punish it under the late act of Parliament. The end cannot sanctify the means. With a view to check this action of an arbitrary rule of Parliament we understand a small squadron is about to sail for the coast of Africa and Brazil ; and we hope soon to see an end to the humbug in our courts þÿ not courts of admiralty þÿ of bringing vessels here

under suspicion only, that they were to be nsed at some period as slavers. The interests of our planters of the Southern States are entirely opposed to the introduction of foreign slaves, because their resources in that way arc amply sufficient for their wants, and because a further supply would diminish the value of those they have. It would then have been our policy to have joined the General Convention of the European States for the entire extinction of the Slave Trade. But with thejeelousy which has marked all our negociations on the subject of maritime rights, we peremptorily declined all or any part in the conversation, as implying a right of search, which might lead to abuse and heart burnings. The offence, however, was made one of high penal character, to our citizens, when caught in the act, and is punishable as piracy þÿ that is by death. We repeat again that these captures are an abrogation of onr laws, if the vessels captured are honafide American vessels ; and if the contrary, why bring them here for adjudication instead of Sierra Leone, the usual port of adjudication for all captures made under the British fla. I he courtesy claimed for the British Admiral on that station we look upon as a mere blind to the infringement of an article of solemn treaty, founded on an act of Parliament, made and passed without the slightest regard to said treaty, or the courtesies usually hud between friendly powers.

The Commerce contains a letter from St. Petersburgh, with the detail of the taking of the Circassian fortress of Akulko We have this day received letters from Tiflis, which give the details of a great check experienced by the Russians in the war with the Circassians, General Gradde (the same

3DAW3K TizstrrwmitSK ma»axa$35Tt>3 ATI?-, to whom an order has been sent to negociate a treaty of peace, or an armistice with these mountaineers), having besieged for 3 months in the fortress of Akulko, which held out obstinately, and wishing to obtain immediate possession of this place, which he considered to be of great importance, had sent for a portion of the army of the Black Sea, consisting of the 20th and 21st division of infantry, J ' a large body of cavalry, and four batteries of artillery, and commenced the assault on the morning of the 1st September. After the Russians had been four times repulsed with loss, the 20th division, which was commanded by General Galaficf, succeeded in penetiating into the fortress by a breach, and then began a sanguinary combat, which lasted until half past 11 o'clock at night, at which time the Circassian garrison yielding to superior numbers, fled under cover of the dark ness, leaving 502 dead, and 121 wounded, of whom the greater number were recognised to be deserters from the army of the Black Sea. The Russians lost in this affair 5850 men in killed and wounded. At the moment when the Russian troops entered the fortress of Akulk, Scamadi, chief of the Circassian tribe of the Tchertchenzes, came up with his cavalry, but arriving, too late too relieve the place, he threw himself upon the Russian cavalry, which he defeated entirely, and took possession of 12 pieces of artillery, which they abandoned after having spiked them. The total loss of the Russian may be esti-

mated at 13.000 men The government proclaim the taking of Akulko as a great victory whereas this operation has placed General Grabbe under an impossibility of continuing the war in Circassia until he shall have received reinforcements, particularly in cavalry."

THE BRITISH TRIUMPH IN INDIA. (From the Morning Herald ) The news from India is well fitted to excite a strong feeling of satisfaction throughout England. The British army of the Indus lias achieved a series of triumphs worthy to be classed along with the unforgotten glories of the Peninsular war. To the officers and men composing that þÿarmy and more especially to its distinguished commander the deep þÿ

gratitude of the country is due. Sir John iveane has proved himself no unworthy pupil of the Duke of Wellington. Higher piaise can scarcely be accorded to the gallant general. The glorious issue of the war will, we trust be turned to good account ; and, beyond ail question, the fall of Ghiznee, and the dethronement of Dost Moharncd, will tend, in a very remarkable degree, to consolidate and extend the influence of England throughout the greater part of Asia. þÿ - þÿ IMPORTANT NEWS FROM INDIA.

The dispatches brought bv this rnnvevarce announce brilliant successes on the pan of the Indian army. Her Majesty's troops marched from Candahar in four divisions on the 27th, 28th, and 2l'.h of May. and on the 3d of June, and arrived, on ti c ! Gth of July, at Mokeer, four days' march from Ghuznee. Up to the 20th insi. it had encountered no more formidable obslaeie than a troop belonging to the rebel tunc, which it repulsed without difficulty. On the 20th the army was concentrated at Nance, 12 ntilcs from Ghuznee, and on t lie 2 1st arrived at that place When within gun shot it was received by a smart cannonade and a heavy fire of musketry, alter silencing which the army bivouacked. On the 22d, preparations were made for assaulting the town, and the attack on it commenced a few minutes before three o'clock on the ensuing morning The gates were blown in by the engineers, and the trumpets having sounded a charge, the artillery opened a terrible fire, under cover of which the infantry forced an entrance in spite of the most determined resistance, and by five o'clock the colours of her Majesty's 13th and 17th regiments floated over the "citadel of Ghuznee. From the Globe. BANK OF STOCKHOLM. The Government of Sweden first established this Bank in 1657. No stock was created ; but instead of tins, three hundred thousand specie crowns were borrowed by the Government, as its capital, and promissory notes wet"" given tor tins money, payable it sight to bearer, and carrying interest. What was thus borrowed at four per cent, was J. nned at six, upon mortgage, and sometimes upon pledges. The Batik was thus at once a bank of circulation, of loan, and of pledges or pawns This last would he called in Europe< a mont d' piele, or Loudon d Honk. The adniinb'tra'iou of this bank was conducted with great li b'iitv, and in fifty years it had acquired a fund of fifty millions. The Government, not satisfied with this prosperous e< initio.! of the bank, nr being com o.i (| to me o an increased expenditure, established i new oank into which the former v\us incorporated It issued notes payable in copper ecus of about six cents value. þÿ More liberal in its discounts than the old one, this hank made urge advances of its own paper to the Government and the nobility- In a short time it had issued notes to the value of six hundred million ecus, or one bundled million dolls. This vast circulation of paper money in Sweden produced the same results which a like circulation has caused in all other countries' A taste for luxury and expense ili'ifused itseit among all classes of society ; the State increased its debt; property holders were ruined ; coin disappeared from circula-

tion. This state of public distress continued until the accession of Gustavus 111., when he restored the credit of the bank by reducing its circulation, forbidding future issues, and bv declaring its notes to he payable in silver. For this purp isc, he had borrowed in Holland a latge amount of silver in ingots. The cm lit of the hank was restored, and its notes again passed at their nominal value. The exigencies of the Stale again required increased expenditures, to meet which largo emissions of pap.T money were made, which cost nothing. This must ever be the means ol paying extraordinary debts by banns or

These vast issues of notes brought with them their necessary attendants þÿ a swift & ruinous depreciations of the notes, and the total disappearance of specie from circulation. I'lie necessities of trade required the use of small money tor change, and as specie had disappeared, the bank found it necessary to issue paper tickets, of verv low denomination, which in the United States are termened sliinpluslers. St. Croix Chhistiansted, (Thursday) 2Gth Dec. 1839. London dates of the 15th ultimo are received pr. 2d November packet. A serious insurrection of the Chartists in Wales broke out early in that month. A mob of several thousands collected and marched to attack the town ol Newport where the magistrates were assembled. They were harangued by the latter, and the riot act was read to them, but this did not make them desist, and they commenced firing on the hotel where the magistrates were assembled. A company of regulars then in the town were called in and returned the lire, when the mob retreated leaving about 25 killed and 59 wounded of their number. Since which the military have been reinforced by squadrons of Cavalry and Artillery, and a number of the ringleaders arrested at.d held to trial. The conspiracy among the Chartists is said to be very extensive.

The Liverpool Steamer arrived at Liverpool X member 7th, and the news of the suspension of the United States Bank and others, caused, as was expected, great excitement in England The London papers are very severe in their comments against that institution. As regards the Bank of England no apprehension of suspension of specie payment appeared to he entertained; their stock was at 179 The British Government stocks remained firm and steady. The rate of interest is stated to be from 6 to 8 pr. Cent pr. annum In the East no change has occurred. The English and French Heels were ahout separating. '1 lie new French Ambassador to Constantinople (Ue Pontois) had arrived, and he has complained of the coldness of his re. ception, particularly by Lord Ponsonhy the British minister, who has let him know that England will in no way join the intrigues of France to support Meliomet Ali in his usurpation. The latter is stated to be much embarrassed for money to pay his armv and fleet, and the possession of the Turish fleet only adds to his burthens. The Biitish victoiy jit India operates favorably for England both in regard to the Egyptian and the Chinese question. The Government of Great Britain have, it is said, decided against paying the

amount of losses for opium seized by the Chinese. This question will ptobably be settled by parliament. In Spain Espartero advances very cautionsly, drawing a circle around Cabrera. From the New York Journal of Commerce, November Xiti, 1839. Great Britain and China. þÿ The London Morning Chronicle of the '2nd inst. contains the following article respecting the relations of Great Britain with China, which is entitled to greater consideration from the fact that the paoer from which it is quoted, is understood to be. to a certain extent, in the contidence of the British government. The course which should be adopted by the British government in regard to the settlement of the opium question is in our minds no longer attended with doubt. Capt. Elliot has now solemly charged the Chinese government as accessories to ihe opium traffic, and as being regular parties to its existence, drawing profits annually from thatjbranch of foreign trade. If such be the case, we at once repudiate the most remote intention of making the people of this country suffer to the extent of one farthing of the loss. The British g ivernment should at once take a decisive course, and insist lor indemnification from the Chinese government to the fullest extent þÿ VVc doubt not that Captain Elliot is prepared to make good his words, and therefore we consider the case free from further obscurity. A sufficient naval and military force should be dispatched at once to Canton to seek for reparation, and, if not granted when demanded, the expedition should immediately disembark their troops, and the licet sail up the river. This, vve understand, will be an object of no very difficult accomplishment. If it be ascertained that the Chinese authorities sanc-

tioned this traffic, the first duty of the British Government is to let it be seen that its subjects shall not be wronged with impunity. The question is one of fact. Foreigners can only know the laws of a country with which they traffic, by the interpretation given to them by the government functionaries of that country ; and if the Chinese functionaries, for a long series of years, have allowed and profited by the trade in opiuin, the question how far they were justified iri allowing and profiting by tins trade is one between thein and their goveminent, with which the foreign traders have no concern. It would be monstrous if a government were to be allowed to take advantage of the wrong of its own officers. þÿ True, that opiuin was contraband ; we have frequently admitted that it was so, by the letter of the Chinese law. But when the people of one country have traded openly and with impunity with those of another for forty years, the usage becomes the law. The device which the Chinese government contrived, to shield themselves from their participation in, and encouragement of, the opium trade, was to hold the Hong merchants responsible that the foreign ships had no opium on hoard ; but, on the other hand these very persons bought the opium regularly The Chinese authorities knew that they did so, and exacted heavy contributions from them for permission to carry on that lucrative branch of foreign trade, and were as much implicated as the importers of the drug þÿ much more so in

fact, because, had it not been for the encouragement which they afforded to the traffic, the demand could not have existed, and the culture of the poppy would not have been carried on to the extent which it has been, in order to supply the Chinese market. We therefore consider that the seizure and destruction of the opium was a most unjustifiable act of spoliation on the part of the Imperial

Commissioner and his associates, and that the government of this country is bound to insist that the British merchants who were the owners of the article shall be fully indemnified by the Chinese government. We sav so as regards the past. The future is open for arrangement ; and if ihe Chinese make it a condition of our renewed intercourse that the trade in opium shall cease or be legalised, the ground is open for considering those conditions. But taking the whole case as regards our last forty years' intercourse into consideration and the decided charge of Captain Elliot, that the traffic in opium has been " cliieflv encouraged and protected by the highest officers in the empire," we deem it clear that the people of this country ought not to pay one farthing of tiie loss which has been sustained by the destruction ol the surrendered opium, and that the British government will act with shameful pusillanimity if they do not obtain full anil peremptory satisfaction from ihe Chinese executive. The sure course to ifo so is to take the high hand with these cunning and self conceited people. To induce them to aci justly, they must be taught to feel ihe necessity of submission ; and if thev hesitate to make full reparation for the loss which our merchants have sustained by the destruction of their property, a British force ought to teach them that British merchants are not to be despoiled of their property with impunity

Frotn the New Orleans Times of the 21th ult. AjjUcting News from Florida þÿ The ship Gen. Washington, Capt. Marburv, arrived here yesterday, in the unprecended short passage of two days from Tampa Bay, to our Levee, brings terrible and atllicting news. þÿ It is stated that the yellow fever iiad been raging with immense effect, not only at St. Augustine, but Tampa Bay, two places hitherto considered the healthiest on the continent. Since the 7th of this month, the U. S. Army in Florida has lost ten of in r biavest and most experienced officers þÿ throwing a gloom into the camp as if the echo of the destroyer's footsteps were heard hourly. At Tampa Bay, General Taylor is reported lying at the point of death, as is also Capt. Barker and I'yton both most distinguished in their profession of arms, and to their courage joining a local expeiience of the Florida region, which others who took their places have yet to learn, Mrs. Sewell is also dead the wile of the Commandant at Tampa Bay. The deaths among the soldiers in camp had been aboul vc per diem. At St. Augustine there had died, Lieuts. Powell and Jennings, both brave and beloved; Midshipman Smith, of the Navy ; Captain Mc'Crubb, and Lieut. Rodney ; also Purser Slocum. Among the passengers in the Washington, were Mrs. Captain Barker and live children þÿ a family most bereaved by the death of their protector. Captain Jewelt also, who from one of the most healthy, strong, and robust men, is now reduced by the fever to a

very shadow. We sincerely condole with the private sufferings and regrets of the personal friends of the deceased; wlnlc as Americans, we weep at the heavy losses which have occurred to the army. Had they died on the field of battle fighting for their country, some consolation would be left for

those who survive them as afflicted friends. But alas, they fell from the insidious attacks of fever þÿ creeping stealthily upon them when they feared no danger, and alllictiug their companions both in camp and by the fireside, when they apprehended no loss. Peace to the soldier's names.

The New York Observer has been favored with the sight of a large number of pictures from a collection of the exquisitely beautiful results of this wonderful discovery, just arrived from Paris, several of them by Daguerre himself. The collection is in the hands of M. Gourraud, a gentleman of taste, who arrived in the steam packet British Queen, and who made himself acquainted with the mode of obtaining these results under the immediate instruction of M. Daguerre. M Gourraud is on his way to the Havana for the purpose of transmitting to Paris photographic views of the scenery of that part of the world. Of the excellence and beauty of these pictures, the Observer says : þÿ Our readers may suppose that, after reading the highly wrought descriptions of the new art, winch we have transferred to our paper from European prints, we were prepared to form something like an adequate conception of i's powers ; but we can only say as the Queen ol Sheba said alter examining the exhibition of the glory of Solomon, "The half was not told us." We can find no language to express the charm ol these not pictures painted to by learn surprised no mortal hand. We are that I' ranee and all Europe arc so enthusiastically interested in the woudefful discovery.

We are told that the shop- windows in Paris, in which the photographic pictures are exhibited, are so beset by the crowd that the streets are impassable in their vicinity. M. Daguetre, we are also informed, is wholly occupied in answering the letters simply of the various sovereigns of Europe, who ail scent anxious to understand the new art. We hope M. Gourraud will stay so long among us as to give us a few practical lectures; and also to furnish an opportunity to our citizens of taste to see this collection of Nature's own paintings.

Education. þÿ Parents, educate your children ! It is the first of your political duties þÿ you owe it to your principles, to your institutions, to your prosperity and to mankind. If you love your country and wish to see her free institutions perpetuated, and her liberty preserved, then educate your children ! Aid so far as lies in your power, in the education of every child in the land. There is no check, upon aristocracy so effectual as the general diffusion of knowledge. A people we'll educated will never be the slaves of tyiants, or the tools of demagogues. Then educate your children ! Those who have aimed to subvert the liberty or abuse the confidence of a free people have approached them through their ignorance. When the bloody M otitis overran the fair province of New Grenada, the course he took to exterminate the seeds of liberty and crush the gernt of revolution, was to put to death every man who could read and write. The test he wisely thought would be tame slaves. To discourage schools and check the progress of knowledge, is one object with most crown heads to Europe. American parents ! þÿ fViends of liberty! let the principles and acts of these men be to vou an impiessive and warning lesson. If tyrants are so well aware that ignorance is the foundation of their power, with what zeal and perseverance ought the friends of liberty to promote and increase the extension of knowledge. This is the prop which sustains all free institutions, and the lever which over-

turns the oppressor's throne. Then educate your children þÿ warn their young feet from the paths of ignorance. Ignorance is the rock on which tyrants build. It was not Ca-sar that overturned the liberties of Rome þÿ it was ignorance. It was not Napoleon that made France a despotism--it was ignorance. It is ignorance keeps Europe in bondage. Ambition has found the broad rock even on American soil, bordering on our own happy country, and would erect thereos a despotism more terrible than that of the wretched Montezuma. Then while monarch At usurpers understand their own interest and preserve it by extinguishing the lamp of knowledge, and punishing with death the free expression of pnbiic opinion be ye not blind to the means of perpetuating and preserving your own liberties. Bind the minds of men in the chains of ignorance and it requires but a moderate portion of art and talents to enslave their bodies. Remove every fragment upon which ambition can seize to erect his gloomy edifice. I repeat it is the first of v«tur political duties þÿ you owe it to your principles, to your institutions, to posterity and to mankind. FREEDOM.
